summary: Gives better guidance for choosing RTCP canonical names (CNAMEs), the persistent identifiers that tie an RTP endpoint's media streams together. The guidance in RFC 3550 was not enough to make names reliably unique within a session, so this document updates it, building on the earlier work in RFC 6222.

plainLanguage.summary: Real-time media sessions need a label that says which streams belong to the same participant. This document explains how to make that label, so that it does not clash with anyone else's and does not let a stranger watch the same participant across different sessions.

subtitle: How to pick the identifier that ties an endpoint's media streams together.

tldr.problem: RTCP CNAMEs are meant to be unique within an RTP session, but the RFC 3550 advice, fully qualified domain names or IPv4 addresses, often produces duplicates, and the RFC 6222 replacement was complicated and could be linked across sessions.
tldr.mechanism: An endpoint builds its CNAME from a UUID, for a long-term persistent name, or from a cryptographically pseudorandom value of at least 96 bits encoded in Base64, for a short-term persistent or per-session name.
tldr.outcome: CNAMEs are unique with very high probability and simpler to generate. This document replaces RFC 6222 and updates RFC 3550.

today: RFC 7022 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2013. It obsoletes RFC 6222 and updates RFC 3550, so it is the current guidance for choosing an RTCP CNAME.

sections.title: What an RTCP CNAME Is For
sections.content:
Section 6.5.1 of RFC 3550 gives a number of recommendations for choosing a unique RTCP CNAME for an RTP endpoint. In practice, some of those methods are not guaranteed to produce a unique CNAME. RFC 6222 updated the guidelines, superseding those in RFC 3550. Unfortunately, some parts of the new algorithms are rather complicated, and they also produce CNAMEs that in some cases are potentially linkable over multiple RTCP sessions even when a new CNAME is generated for each session. This document specifies a replacement for the algorithm in Section 5 of RFC 6222, which does not have that limitation and is simpler to implement.

The CNAME is the label an RTP endpoint puts in its RTCP reports, so that the other participants in a session can tell which media streams belong to the same endpoint. An RTP endpoint emits one or more RTP streams, each with its own synchronization source identifier, and the CNAME ties those together for the receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: Real-time media sessions need a label that says which streams belong to the same participant. This document explains how to make that label, so that it does not clash with anyone else's and does not let a stranger watch the same participant across different sessions.

sections.title: Why the Earlier Advice Fell Short
sections.content:
The recommendation in RFC 3550 is to generate an RTCP CNAME of the form "user@host" for multiuser systems, or "host" if the username is not available, with the host part being the fully qualified domain name of the host from which the real-time data originates. While that guidance was appropriate when RFC 3550 was written, fully qualified domain names are no longer necessarily unique and can sometimes be common across several endpoints in large service provider networks. This document replaces the use of the domain name as an RTCP CNAME by alternative mechanisms.

IPv4 addresses are also suggested in RFC 3550, where the host part of the CNAME is the numeric address of the interface the data comes from. As RFC 3550 itself notes, the use of private network address space can result in hosts having addresses that are not globally unique. The same sharing of one address can occur with public IPv4 addresses if several hosts are assigned the same public address and are connected to a Network Address Translation device. Where several hosts share the same address, whether private or public, using the address as the CNAME leads to CNAMEs that are not necessarily unique.

RFC 3550 also notes that if hosts with private addresses and no direct IP connectivity to the public Internet have their RTP packets forwarded to the public Internet through an RTP-level translator, they could end up with non-unique CNAMEs. Its suggestion is that such applications provide a configuration option allowing the user to choose a unique CNAME, which puts the burden on the translator to translate CNAMEs from private addresses to public addresses so that private addresses are not exposed. Experience has shown that this does not work well in practice.

For the same reasons, using the numeric representation of the IPv4 address as the host part of the CNAME is NOT RECOMMENDED. It is difficult, and in some cases impossible, for a host to determine whether there is a NAT between itself and its RTP peer, and even some public IPv4 addresses can be shared by multiple hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: The old advice was to use the machine's domain name or its IP address. Neither works now: domain names are often shared by many machines in a large network, and IP addresses are shared whenever a network address translator puts several machines behind one public address. Two machines can therefore end up with the same label.

sections.title: Persistent or Per-Session
sections.content:
The RTCP CNAME can either be persistent across different RTP sessions for an RTP endpoint, or unique per session, meaning that the endpoint chooses a different CNAME for each RTP session.

An RTP endpoint that emits multiple related RTP streams requiring synchronization at the other endpoint MUST use the same CNAME for all the streams that are to be synchronized. That requires a short-term persistent CNAME common across several RTP streams and potentially across several related sessions. A common example is syncing audio and video streams in a multimedia session, where one participant has to use the same CNAME for its audio session and its video session. Another is synchronizing the layers of a layered audio codec, where the same CNAME has to be used for each layer. If the multiple RTP streams in a session are not related and do not require synchronization, an endpoint can use different CNAMEs for them.

A longer-term persistent CNAME is sometimes useful to facilitate third-party monitoring, consistent with RFC 3550. One use would be to let network management tools correlate the ongoing quality of service for a participant across multiple sessions for fault diagnosis and to understand long-term network performance statistics. An application developer that wishes to discourage this kind of third-party monitoring can choose to generate a unique CNAME for each session, or group of related sessions, that the application will join. Such a per-session CNAME cannot be used for traffic analysis, and so provides some limited form of privacy. There are non-RTP means that a third party can use to correlate RTP sessions, so per-session CNAMEs will not prevent a determined traffic analyst from monitoring them.

It is possible, and legitimate, for independent implementations to make different choices of CNAME when running on the same host. That can hinder third-party monitoring, unless some external means is provided to configure a persistent choice for those implementations. There is no backwards compatibility issue with implementations that follow RFC 3550, since the CNAMEs are opaque strings to remote peers.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two habits. A participant can keep the same label for a long time, which lets a network manager watch its quality over time, or it can use a fresh label for every session, which keeps a stranger from linking the sessions together. The label must be the same across the audio and video streams of one call, because those have to stay in step.

sections.title: The Three Ways to Choose One
sections.content:
An RTP endpoint wishing to generate a persistent CNAME MUST use one of two methods. To produce a long-term persistent CNAME, the endpoint MUST generate and store a Universally Unique IDentifier (UUID) for use as the host part of its CNAME. The UUID MUST be version 1, 2 or 4 as described in RFC 4122, with the "urn:uuid:" prefix stripped, resulting in a 36-octet printable string representation.

To produce a short-term persistent CNAME, the endpoint MUST generate and use an identifier by following the procedure in Section 5. That procedure is performed at least once per initialization of the software. After obtaining an identifier, minimally the least significant 96 bits SHOULD be converted to ASCII using Base64 encoding, to compromise between packet size and uniqueness. If 96 bits are used, the resulting string is 16 octets, and the Base64 encoded value cannot exceed the maximum RTCP CNAME length of 255 octets.

In both cases, the "user@" part of the CNAME MAY be omitted on single-user systems and MAY be replaced by an opaque token on multiuser systems, to preserve privacy.

An RTP endpoint wishing to generate a per-session CNAME MUST generate a new one for every new RTP session, following the procedure in Section 5 and then converting minimally the least significant 96 bits to ASCII using Base64. The CNAME cannot change over the life of an RTP session, and the "user@" part is omitted for per-session CNAMEs.

Obtaining uniqueness, with a high probability, is an important property that requires careful evaluation of the method. The document provides a number of methods, at least one of which would suit any given deployment scenario, and so it does not leave the implementor to define and select an alternative method. A future specification might define an alternative, as long as the method has appropriate uniqueness and there is consistency between the methods used for multiple sessions that are to be correlated, but such a specification needs to be reviewed and approved before deployment. The mechanisms here are for generating RTCP CNAMEs, and are not to be used for generating general-purpose unique identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: Three recipes are given. For a name that lasts a long time, store a UUID and use it. For a name that lasts as long as the program runs, or for a fresh name each session, take a random value, keep at least 96 bits of it and write those bits in Base64.

sections.title: Generating the Identifier
sections.content:
To produce a unique identifier locally, one simply generates a cryptographically pseudorandom value as described in RFC 4086. This value MUST be at least 96 bits.

The biggest bottleneck to implementing this algorithm is the availability of an appropriate cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator. In any setting that already has a secure generator, this algorithm is far simpler than the one in Section 5 of RFC 6222. SIP stacks are required to use cryptographically random numbers to generate To and From tags. Real-Time Communications on the Web implementations will need secure generators to implement ICE and DTLS-SRTP. And essentially every web browser already supports TLS, which requires a secure generator.
sections.plainLanguage: Making the random value is the only hard part, and most systems already have what is needed: a browser has TLS, a SIP stack has random tags, and a web calling stack already makes random keys. The rest is a matter of writing 96 bits down in Base64.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3550 apply to this document. For random CNAMEs, the recommendations given ensure that a set of cooperating participants in an RTP session will, with very high probability, have unique CNAMEs. Neither RFC 3550 nor this document provides any way to ensure that participants choose their CNAMEs appropriately, so implementations MUST NOT rely on the uniqueness of CNAMEs for any essential security service. This matches RFC 3550, which does not require that CNAMEs are unique within a session but says that condition SHOULD hold. Because each participant in a session is free to choose its own CNAME, it can do so in a way that impersonates another participant; participants are trusted not to impersonate each other, and no recommendation for generating CNAMEs can prevent this, because an attacker can ignore the stipulation. Secure RTP keeps unauthorized entities out of an RTP session, but it does not aim to prevent impersonation attacks from authorized entities.

Because of the properties of the generator, there is no significant privacy or linkability difference between long and short CNAMEs. However, the requirement to generate unique CNAMEs implies a certain minimum length. A length of 96 bits allows on the order of 2^40 CNAMEs globally before there is a large chance of collision, and there is about a 50% chance of one collision after 2^48 CNAMEs.

Earlier recommendations for CNAME generation allowed a fixed value, which lets an attacker easily link separate RTP sessions, removing the obfuscation that IPv6 privacy addresses or IPv4 Network Address Port Translation provide. This specification no longer describes a procedure to generate fixed CNAME values, so CNAME values no longer provide that linkage. That was necessary to remove the linking by an attacker, but of course it complicates linking by traffic analysis devices, such as devices looking for dropped or delayed packets.
sections.plainLanguage: A name that is unique is not a proof of identity: a participant could deliberately copy someone else's name, so nothing that depends on security may rely on the name being unique. The random values are long enough that clashes are very unlikely, and because the name changes from session to session it no longer tells a watcher which sessions belong to the same person.

items.title: Fully qualified domain name
items.text: No longer necessarily unique, and can be common across several endpoints in large service provider networks.

items.title: IPv4 address
items.text: Private addresses are not globally unique, and public addresses can be shared by several hosts behind a NAT device.

items.title: RTP-level translator
items.text: Hosts behind one can end up with the same CNAME, and translating CNAMEs at the translator does not work well in practice.

viz.caption: THE THREE WAYS TO CHOOSE AN RTCP CNAME

items.label: Long-term persistent
items.desc: Generate and store a UUID of version 1, 2 or 4, with the urn:uuid: prefix stripped, giving a 36-octet printable string as the host part.

items.label: Short-term persistent
items.desc: Generate an identifier by the Section 5 procedure at least once per initialization of the software, then Base64 encode at least the least significant 96 bits, giving a 16-octet string.

items.label: Per-session
items.desc: Generate a new identifier for every new RTP session by the Section 5 procedure and Base64 encode at least the least significant 96 bits. The user part is omitted.
